title: The animals
hookLine: he told of a sinner forgiven for giving water to a thirsty dog (Bukhari)

cards: A man is walking a desert road on a brutally hot day, desperate for water. He finds a well, climbs down, drinks, and climbs back up. At the top is a dog, panting, so thirsty it's licking the damp mud around the well.
The man thinks: this dog is feeling exactly what I felt a minute ago. He has no bucket, no cup. What would you do?
Walk on? It's a dog, and you've had your drink. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told this story, and the ending surprised his companions so much they had to ask him a question.

teach.b: The man climbed back down the well. He filled his leather sock with water, held it in his teeth so he could climb with both hands, came up, and gave the dog a drink.
The Prophet said, in Sahih al-Bukhari: God thanked him for it, and forgave him. The companions asked: messenger of God, is there really a reward for us in animals?

He answered with a line Muslims still quote: in every living creature there is reward. Another version, also in Bukhari, makes it sharper: the one who gave the water was a woman known for sin, and she was forgiven for it.

The Prophet told the other side too. A woman locked up a cat, didn't feed it, and didn't let it go to find food, until it died, and he said she was punished for it. The same care shows up in his own life.
Companions on a journey once took two chicks from a nest, and the mother bird circled over them in distress.
The Prophet asked, who has troubled this bird by taking her young?
Give them back to her. And one day in a garden in Medina a camel saw him and moaned, with tears in its eyes.
He went to it and stroked it until it calmed, then found its owner and said: don't you fear God concerning this animal? It has told me you starve it and wear it out.
The Qur'an says that every creature on earth and every bird on two wings are communities, like you.

how: Some Muslims leave water out for birds and stray animals in hot weather, citing the hadith of the thirsty dog, and Islamic legal works set out duties of care toward working and domestic animals.

o: the Prophet's teaching of reward in caring for every creature
the Qur'an's rules on which animals are lawful to eat
the camels and horses the Prophet kept in Medina

games.q: what's inside the stories — tap the pairs.
p: water carried in a leather sock
locked up and left to die
give her young back to her

s: the man in the story was forgiven for watering a dog
God thanked him and forgave him, says Sahih al-Bukhari.
the companions assumed there was reward in animals
they were surprised and asked; he said in every living creature there is reward.
the Qur'an calls animals and birds communities

games.q: you've climbed out of a well after drinking. a dog is dying of thirst at the top. you have no bucket. what do you do?
o: walk on. it's only a dog.
climb back down and bring water in your sock.
call for someone else to help it.
games.why: he climbed down, filled his leather sock, carried it in his teeth, and watered the dog. God thanked him and forgave him.

practice: Put out water for an animal, or plan it: a bowl on the step, a dish in the yard, fresh water for a pet whose bowl you haven't checked.
Then think of the animals near you that you mostly don't notice, birds on the wire, a neighbor's dog, the cat in the alley, and picture each one, for a moment, as a community of its own.

wordCard.voice: The animals. The Prophet's teaching that there's reward in every living creature, from a thirsty dog to a grieving bird. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: in every moist liver there is reward, meaning every living creature.

carryVoice: Your line: water for the dog. Even a small kindness to an animal counts. Day two hundred seventy-two, done.
